lesson.title: Where the Outputs Land: Understanding Range
lesson.summary: The range of a function is the complete set of output values it actually produces, the natural counterpart to domain that focuses on results instead of inputs.
lesson.body:
If domain describes every value you are allowed to feed into a function, range describes every value that can come back out. Formally, the range of a function is the set of all output values that actually result from plugging in every input in the domain. Range and domain are always discussed as a pair, one describing the inputs and one describing the outputs, and getting comfortable telling them apart is one of the more important habits in this unit, since they answer two different questions about the exact same function.

For a function described by a short list of ordered pairs, finding the range works the same way finding the domain does, except now you collect the second coordinates instead of the first. For the function (1, 4), (2, 7), (3, 4), (4, 10), the second coordinates are 4, 7, 4, and 10, but since 4 repeats, you list it only once, giving a range of 4, 7, and 10. Notice that repeated outputs are completely fine for a function, as established earlier, so a repeated value in the range never signals a problem.

Range becomes trickier for a function defined by a formula, because you have to think about what values the output expression can actually reach, not just what you can plug in. Consider f(x) = x^2. No matter what real number you substitute for x, positive, negative, or zero, squaring it always produces a result that is zero or positive; it is mathematically impossible to square a real number and land on something negative. So the range of f(x) = x^2 is all real numbers greater than or equal to 0. Check this with a few values: f(0) = 0^2 = 0, f(3) = 3^2 = 9, and f(-3) = (-3)^2 = 9 as well. Every output is 0 or positive, and every non-negative number, like 9, is reachable, which is exactly what the range describes.

Now consider g(x) = x + 5, an ordinary linear function with domain of all real numbers. Because you can substitute any real number for x, and adding 5 shifts every possible input up by exactly 5, the output can also be any real number at all; there is no value the output could ever be blocked from reaching. So the range of g(x) = x + 5 is all real numbers, matching its domain. This example shows that domain and range do not always restrict each other the same way; a function can have an unlimited domain and still have a limited range, as with x^2, or have both domain and range be completely unrestricted, as with a straight line.

Reading a graph is often the fastest way to identify range visually: the domain is everything the graph covers left to right along the x-axis, while the range is everything the graph covers bottom to top along the y-axis. Getting practiced at separating these two directions, horizontal for domain and vertical for range, will make the next several concepts, input, output, and function notation, feel like natural extensions of ideas you already have rather than brand new rules to memorize.
